newsitem.title: UK: Sicily wants to shed Mafia image to lure investors.
newsitem.headline: Sicily wants to shed Mafia image to lure investors.

text.p: Sicily's centre-right government is embracing Thatcherite economic policies but needs to shed its image as a centre for organised crime to attract investors, Sicily's president said on Friday.
"Sicily requires a dose of Thatcherite policies. The heavy involvement of the government in companies has to be reduced," Guiseppe Provenzano, president of Sicily, told Reuters in an interview.
"In order to encourage flows of investments (from abroad) the first requirement is to change the image of Sicily," he said.
He said the Sicilian Mafia was often the only aspect of the autonomous Italian region that was known to the outside world.

Sicily's centre-right coalition, which came to power last year after 30 years of socialist rule, has introduced measures to cut the region's expenditure and passed legislation to sell off many of its companies.
"We have started the drive to privatise all sectors of the economy, including finance, tourism, industry and mining," Provenzano, a former economics professor, said.

"Legal guidelines have been completed and the process will start soon. Within two years privatisation should be completed. It will be done mainly through sales to other companies, because most enterprises are not large enough for a stock exchange flotation," he said.

"To attract finance we have implemented labour cost and tax incentives. Sicily offers very favourable opportunities for investment because the state is retreating and there is a lot to be done in terms of infrastructure," he said, adding Sicily was already attracting substantial funds from the European Union.
Margaret Thatcher, Britain's prime minister between 1979 and 1990, radically reformed the country with free-market policies which included privatisation, income tax cuts and welfare state reform.
"Sicily has a lot of autonomy from the Italian state and this gives us considerable leeway and the possibility of developing the island on the principles of free markets," Provenzano said.
"The grain of these policies will go against vested (Mafia) interests but this is the only way forward for Sicily," he said.

The strength of the Mob has been battered by a series of key Mafia arrests. Last week, Pietro Aglieri, one of Italy's three most wanted men, was arrested. Last year Sicilian boss Giovanni Brusca was also captured.
"It has been true, and perhaps still is true, that Sicily is the capital of the Mafia, but it is also the centre of the war against the Mafia," Provenzano said.
"The strength of the anti-Mafia movement is reflected in recent successes by police against them," he said.
Provenzano was in London to sign a 1.7 trillion lire ($1 billion) loan arranged via investment bank Credit Suisse First Boston. The Sicilian government aims to balance its budget by next year.

"Three months ago we created a legal framework to access the international capital markets. The first step has already been taken. The next step is to refinance 800 billion lire of loans into cheaper funds," he said.
Sicily is one of five regions within Italy with greater political, administrative and legislative autonomy but the only one to collect taxes directly.
For the first time in history the regional government is different to the state government, currently a centre-left coalition.
But Provenzano said the Italian central government would not find it easy to oppose the region's policies.

"The central government will have to support Sicily because its attitude to us will be seen as a test of its commitment to carrying out reforms in the rest of Italy, many parts of which want more autonomy," he said.
($ = 1697 Italian Lire)
